summary.purpose: Earlier completed CLI route; retained after primary experiment moved to a uniform app sub-agent interface.

rows.title: A New Radio to Overcome Critical Link Budgets

errors.location: Section III, equations (3)–(4), and the claim following equation (3)
errors.description: The stated unitary-waveform model does not provide the claimed T-fold SINR gain. A unitary matrix has rows of unit norm, so correlating the received signal with a row preserves that symbol’s energy; with orthogonal rows, equation (4) isolates each symbol as h_n x_{b,n}. A T-fold gain would require different energy normalization. The same equations do not show coherent combining of N antennas for each independent data symbol, so they do not establish the claimed beamforming-equivalent link-budget gain.
errors.evidence: “If the matrix F_b is unitary, the data symbols x_{b,n} can be recovered without crosstalk by the matched filters f_{b,n}† that provide the T-fold improvement of SINR”; later: “There is no loss in link budget gain compared to spatial beamforming at the transmitter.”

errors.location: Section III, equation (3), and the first numerical example
errors.description: T is used as the dimension of the T×T matrix F_b, so it must be an integer. The first numerical example sets T=18.375, which cannot instantiate the stated finite-dimensional matrix model. No alternative continuous-time definition of F_b is provided to connect that example to the model.
errors.evidence: “F_b ∈ C^{T × T}” followed by “we set T = 18.375.”

errors.location: Final summary bullet beginning “Peak data rate”
errors.description: For a fixed finite number of spatial streams, spatial multiplexing can multiply the number of streams, but it does not make rate grow linearly with SNR in general: the rate remains logarithmic in SNR at high SNR. The manuscript’s own equation (9) gives log₂(1+SNR); its linear approximation applies only at low SNR and is not a benefit specific to spatial multiplexing.
errors.evidence: “Peak data rate can be made to grow linearly with SNR by means of spatial multiplexing”; equation (9) states R = log₂(1 + SNR), and equation (10) labels the linear relation as a low-SNR approximation.

errors.location: Final summary bullet beginning “Diversity is fully exploited”
errors.description: Omnidirectional transmission can make multipath signals available, but it does not by itself ensure that spatial or temporal diversity is fully exploited. That requires independent channel observations and a receiver or coding method that combines them; the cited reasoning establishes only that propagation paths are not excluded by transmit beam direction.
errors.evidence: “Temporal and spatial diversity is fully exploited as the transmit signal is sent omni-directionally, allowing for multi-path propagation without angular restrictions.”

rows.title: Assessing the effect of therapeutic level of oxytetracycline dihydrate on pharmacokinetics and biosafety in Oncorhynchus mykiss (Walbaum, 1792)

errors.location: Materials and methods — AUC trapezoidal formula
errors.description: The stated trapezoidal AUC formula omits the factor of 1/2. As written, each interval contributes twice the standard trapezoid area, so AUC values calculated with this formula would be doubled.
errors.evidence: The manuscript gives AUC = Σ(Cᵢ + Cᵢ₊₁)·(tᵢ₊₁ − tᵢ), without dividing by 2.

errors.location: Results — Pharmacokinetic result; absorption rate constant
errors.description: The reported absorption rate range is inconsistent with the stated equation and the muscle absorption half-life: 17.23 h implies Kₐ ≈ 0.040 h⁻¹, outside the reported range.
errors.evidence: The manuscript states Kₐ = ln(2)/t₁/₂a, gives muscle t₁/₂a as 17.23 h, and reports Kₐ values of 0.0002–0.011 h⁻¹.

errors.location: Results — Pharmacokinetic result; elimination half-lives; Conclusion
errors.description: The reported elimination half-lives conflict, and the conclusion identifies the liver as having the longest half-life despite the Results giving a much longer plasma value.
errors.evidence: The Results give liver t₁/₂b as 238.68 h and later as 420.28 h; they also report plasma at 3368.24 h. The Conclusion calls the liver half-life of 238.68 h the longest.

errors.location: Results — Table 2 validation results
errors.description: The reported R² values do not support the claimed calibration linearity: R² cannot exceed 1, and a value of 0.002 indicates essentially no fit.
errors.evidence: The manuscript reports an R² of 6.96 for muscle and 0.002 for skin, while describing R² as reflecting calibration linearity.

errors.location: Results — Table 2 validation results; Discussion
errors.description: Negative LOD and LOQ values are not physically meaningful concentration limits, so interpreting them as evidence of minimal detectable drug presence is invalid.
errors.evidence: The manuscript reports kidney LOD −587.51 µg kg⁻¹ and LOQ −1780.34 µg kg⁻¹, then states that negative LOD/LOQ values suggest minimal drug presence.

errors.location: Discussion — muscle residue and consumer safety
errors.description: The claim that residues in the 1× and 3× groups remained below the EU MRL conflicts with the reported day-20 maxima, both of which exceed the stated 100 µg kg⁻¹ MRL.
errors.evidence: The manuscript reports day-20 muscle concentrations of 118 µg kg⁻¹ at 1× and 351 µg kg⁻¹ at 3×, then says residues remained below the 100 µg kg⁻¹ MRL in those groups.

errors.location: Results — creatinine; biochemical-results table
errors.description: The baseline creatinine results conflict after unit conversion: 0.2 mg/L equals 0.02 mg/dL, not the 0.05 mg/dL stated for the control group.
errors.evidence: The table gives control creatinine as 0.2 mg/L on day 0; the accompanying text gives the control level as 0.05 ± 0.001 mg/dL.

errors.location: Materials and methods — biosafety dosing; Results — feeding behavior
errors.description: The manuscript reports only 80–90% consumption of medicated feed, while describing the groups by the nominal feed dose. Unless the dose was adjusted for uneaten feed, the fish's actual exposure was below the stated dose, leaving the claimed dose-specific safety assessment uncertain.
errors.evidence: The methods specify doses of 80, 240, 400, and 800 mg kg⁻¹ fish day⁻¹; the Results state that only 80–90% of feed was consumed during medicated feeding.

rows.title: Glycerol-silica/chitosan conjugated self-assembled nano-flower framework for Herstulla thompsoni delivery with effectiveness in natural settings: Optimization and pilot scale production

errors.location: Artemia salina toxicity methods and results
errors.description: The manuscript reports incompatible test concentrations, so the toxicity findings cannot be assigned to a definite exposure dose.
errors.evidence: Methods: acute test solution “(100.0 mg L⁻¹).” Later, the toxicity discussion refers to “100 μg/L,” and the developmental-toxicity results refer to both “100μg/L” and “100 μg/mL HTS_NFG.”

errors.location: Results, pilot-batch characterization; Fig. 4d label
errors.description: The pilot-batch zeta potential is reported with opposite signs. These values cannot both describe the same measurement, and the polarity matters to the stated particle-charge interpretation.
errors.evidence: Text: pilot-scale zeta potential was “31.48mv” and earlier “+31.48 mv”; Fig. 4d label: “Zeta Potential: -31.48 mV.”

errors.location: Degradation-state methods and UV-resistance results
errors.description: The UV assay does not establish that HTS retained biological activity after irradiation. It measures whole-formulation UV–visible spectra, morphology, and particle size, but reports no post-irradiation fungal viability, germination, or insecticidal activity measurement; those observations therefore do not support the conclusion that NFG protects HTS efficacy.
errors.evidence: Methods: after UV exposure, “The UV spectra and morphology of the HTS_NFG were observed” and particle size was monitored. Results: unchanged absorbance is used to conclude that “the self-assembly of NFG provides UV protection to HTS” and enhances UV resistance.

rows.title: ITERTL: An Iterative Framework for Fine-tuning LLMs for RTL Code Generation

errors.location: Section 3.2, Equation 6
errors.description: The derivation equates the negative log probability of an observed token with a KL divergence. These are not equal: KL is an expectation over the teacher’s token distribution, and expected negative log likelihood equals KL plus the teacher’s entropy. The displayed ratio also places `log Pπ` in the denominator. Thus Equation 6 is mathematically incorrect as written, even though the objectives can have the same minimizer under an appropriate expectation.
errors.evidence: “Σ_j -log Pπ(a_j | s, a_{<j}) = … Σ_j KL(P_teacher,j || P_π,j)”

errors.location: Sections 3.1 and 3.2, iterative sampling claim and Equation 8
errors.description: Sampling training responses from π_t does not establish that their distribution mismatch with the optimized model is reduced: training then changes the model to π_{t+1}. The manuscript gives no bound or measurement showing that this change is smaller than the mismatch it replaces, so the stated mitigation is not demonstrated by the derivation.
errors.evidence: “π_{t+1} = argmax_π … E_{a~π_t(.|s)}[r_π(s,a)]”; the text concludes that replacing π_old with π_t “effectively mitigates the distribution mismatch.”

errors.location: Section 4.1, Decoding Strategy
errors.description: Choosing the best result across four temperatures for each test metric can make benchmark scores selection-biased if those same benchmark results determine the chosen temperature. The manuscript does not state that temperature selection was made independently of the evaluation benchmarks.
errors.evidence: “the model is prompted to generate responses with temperature = {0 …, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8} … For each test metric … the best result is chosen.”

rows.title: Farnesoid X receptor activation protects against renal fibrosis via modulation of β-catenin signaling

errors.location: Animal methods; Results; Figure 6 caption
errors.description: The manuscript reports 20 weeks of HFD exposure, but the methods describe 3 weeks before group assignment followed by 12 weeks of treatment. That schedule gives 12 weeks on the assigned diet, not 20; it appears to conflate the mice’s age at study end with HFD duration.
errors.evidence: Methods: mice were purchased at 5 weeks, randomly divided after 3 weeks, and euthanized after a 12-week treatment. Results: “Mice were fed by a 60% kcal fat diet for 20 weeks”; Figure 6 caption: kidneys were from groups “for 20 weeks.”

errors.location: Results—mouse biochemical measurements; Figure 5, panel H
errors.description: Serum creatinine is reported with conflicting units: μmol/L in the results and mmol/L in the Figure 5 panel H label. These units differ by a factor of 1,000, so the reported scale is ambiguous.
errors.evidence: Results: “serum creatinine (4.8 ± 1.3 vs. 1.11 μmol/L)”; Figure 5 panel H label: “Serum Creatinine (mmol/L).”

rows.title: A Relationship Between Nonphysical Quasi-probabilities and Nonlocality Objectivity

errors.location: Definition 1.2; Eqs. (3), (8)–(9); Theorem 1.4
errors.description: The claimed swap-dependent nonlocality cannot follow from the stated criterion. Swapping the qubits changes the correlation matrix from β to βᵀ, but βᵀβ and ββᵀ have the same eigenvalues, so M is unchanged. In the stated row- or column-supported cases, both give eigenvalues (‖b‖², 0, 0); consequently Eq. (9) cannot make one labelling nonlocal and the swapped labelling local.
errors.evidence: Definition 1.2 interchanges the Pauli factors, which transposes the correlation coefficients. Equation (3) uses the two largest eigenvalues of βᵀβ, while Eq. (8) asserts an asymmetry between the row- and column-supported cases.

errors.location: Eqs. (6)–(7); construction in the proof of Theorem 1.4
errors.description: The eigenvalue formulas omit the overall factor 1/4 from the definition of ρ. For example, when all coefficients vanish, Eq. (7) gives four eigenvalues equal to 1, although Eq. (1) gives ρ = I₄/4, whose eigenvalues are 1/4. As a result, the construction's stated distance excess |λ₀| gives an actual minimum eigenvalue −|λ₀|/4, not λ₀.
errors.evidence: Equation (1) defines ρ with prefactor 1/4, but Eqs. (6)–(7) list eigenvalues without that prefactor; Theorem 1.4 identifies λ₀ as the smallest eigenvalue of ρ.

errors.location: Theorem 1.1 and its use of “nonlocal” and “local”
errors.description: The condition in Eq. (3) tests violation of the CHSH inequality, not Bell nonlocality in the unrestricted sense used elsewhere in the manuscript. Failure to violate CHSH does not, by itself, establish a local hidden-variable model for all Bell inequalities and measurements. Thus the stated “iff” and the corresponding general locality claims overreach unless “nonlocal” is restricted to CHSH nonlocality.
errors.evidence: The manuscript introduces an experimentally testable Bell inequality and then states that M > 1 is equivalent to nonlocality, without limiting the claim to violation of that inequality.

rows.title: Efficient Human Pose Estimation: Leveraging Advanced Techniques with MediaPipe

errors.location: Methodology, joint-angle equation; curl-counter logic
errors.description: The subtraction of two atan2 results gives a signed angle that can be negative or fall outside the 0°–180° range. The stated curl thresholds therefore depend on landmark orientation and can misclassify an otherwise identical curl. The angle must be wrapped and converted to an unsigned joint angle before applying these thresholds.
errors.evidence: The angle is defined as `arctan2(c_y - b_y, c_x - b_x) - arctan2(a_y - b_y, a_x - b_x)`; the curl stages use `angle > 160°` and `angle < 30°`.

errors.location: Experimental evaluation, performance metrics
errors.description: IoU is specified as an area-overlap metric, but the described model output consists of landmark coordinates. The manuscript does not define regions or masks derived from those landmarks, ground-truth areas, or an annotation procedure, so the stated IoU evaluation is not defined for the reported outputs as described.
errors.evidence: The model “returns a set of landmark coordinates”; the metrics are listed as `MSE = ...` and `IoU = (Area of Overlap) / (Area of Union)`, with no area construction or ground-truth definition.

errors.location: Experimental results and conclusion
errors.description: The claimed accuracy and speed gains cannot be checked from the supplied results: no baseline or optimized metric values, sample counts, or variability are reported. The stated table has no entries, and the results section leaves “Key statistics include:” blank. Thus the 20% IoU increase and 30% processing-time reduction are unsupported by the presented evidence.
errors.evidence: The results say “Table 1 summarizes” performance but provide only a caption, then say “Key statistics include:” without values. The conclusion nevertheless claims “a 20% increase” in IoU and “a reduction in processing time by approximately 30%.”

rows.title: Illuminating the dark kinome: utilizing multiplex peptide activity arrays to functionally annotate understudied kinases

errors.location: Methods: recombinant EPHA6 construct; Results: EPHA6 mass spectrometry
errors.description: The reported EPHA6 phosphorylation sites cannot be present in the stated recombinant protein fragment. The construct spans residues 683–1130, while the reported sites are Y259 and Y484; neither lies within that fragment.
errors.evidence: “EPH receptor A6 (EPHA6, AA range R683-V1130)” and “two putative autophosphorylation sites on EPHA6 at pY259 and pY484.”

errors.location: Methods: postmortem DLPFC pooling; Results: schizophrenia kinome analysis and sex-specific conclusions
errors.description: Pooling subjects by diagnosis and sex, then running technical triplicates, leaves one biological pool per group. Technical replicates do not provide independent subject-level replication, so the reported sex-specific and diagnosis-related differences cannot establish population-level effects or their biological variability.
errors.evidence: “samples were pooled by diagnosis and sex”; “Each of the four pooled samples”; “Pooled samples were run in technical triplicate”; later, “we observed a strong reduction of global phosphorylation in both male and female subjects.”

errors.location: Methods: recombinant kinase screening; Results: affinity groups
errors.description: The high-, medium-, and low-affinity categories are assigned from the amount of kinase needed to produce a signal on fixed peptide arrays. That enzyme-dose response does not measure substrate-binding affinity or establish an affinity ranking.
errors.evidence: “High Affinity” peptides show activity “at the lowest protein concentration”; “Medium Affinity” peptides begin showing activity “at the medium protein concentration”; “Low Affinity” peptides show activity “at the highest protein concentration.”

errors.location: Results: recombinant kinase screening; Abstract and Conclusion: total interactions
errors.description: The reported affinity-group counts sum to 201 kinase–peptide hits: EPHA6 53, TNK1 63, AATK 65, INSRR 15, and LTK 5. This does not match the claim of 195 kinase–substrate interactions. Overlapping peptide sequences would still represent separate interactions when phosphorylated by different kinases; if 195 instead counts unique peptide sequences, the reported quantity is mislabeled.
errors.evidence: The text reports EPHA6 “18 high,” “31 medium,” and “4 low”; TNK1 “26,” “31,” and “6”; AATK “9,” “46,” and “10”; INSRR “3,” “4,” and “8”; and LTK “3,” “1,” and “1” peptides by affinity group, while the Abstract and Conclusion each claim “195” interactions.

rows.title: MSP-MVS: Multi-granularity Segmentation Prior Guided Multi-View Stereo

errors.location: Introduction, paragraph beginning “Therefore, we propose TSAR-MVS”; related work, paragraph beginning “Different, TAPA-MVS”; conclusion, paragraph beginning “In this paper, we introduce MSP-MVS”
errors.description: The manuscript presents two incompatible methods as its proposed contribution. The introduction identifies TSAR-MVS as the new method and describes confidence filtering, superpixel RANSAC refinement, weighted median filtering, and textureless-aware segmentation. Later, related work lists TSAR-MVS as an existing method, while the abstract and conclusion identify the proposed method as MSP-MVS, based on patch deformation, anchor equidistribution, and iterative local search. The results and contribution claims therefore cannot be unambiguously attributed to one method.
errors.evidence: “Therefore, we propose TSAR-MVS, a generalized post-processing MVS method...” versus “TAPA-MVS ... and TSAR-MVS (Yuan et al. 2024b) attempt to employ superpixel planarization...” and “In this paper, we introduce MSP-MVS...”

errors.location: Patch-deformation discussion, paragraphs beginning “Due to the absence of depth edge as constraints” and “Since APD-MVS lacks depth edge guidance”
errors.description: The method treats Semantic-SAM segmentation boundaries as a source of depth-edge guidance, but the manuscript does not establish that those boundaries correspond to geometric depth discontinuities. It describes them only as boundaries that “may contain potential depth edges.” Without a stated test or criterion separating semantic boundaries from actual depth edges, the claimed depth-edge prior may constrain deformation at boundaries that do not represent depth changes and miss depth changes within a segment.
errors.evidence: “Semantic-SAM can achieve panoramic segmentation at any granularity level, which may contain potential depth edges. Therefore, we attempt to adopt Semantic-SAM to extract multi-granularity depth edges for patch deformation.”

rows.title: Qsyn: A Developer-Friendly Quantum Circuit Synthesis Framework for NISQ Era and Beyond

errors.location: Comparison with PyZX paragraph and Table I heading
errors.description: The manuscript concludes that Qsyn is faster, uses less memory, and produces circuits with equal-or-lower RZ counts and lower average depth, but supplies no table values or experimental protocol in the provided text. The claims of superior performance and a fair comparison therefore cannot be independently assessed from the reported evidence.
errors.evidence: “We demonstrate Qsyn’s superior performance through fair comparisons with PyZX”; “Qsyn tended to optimize circuits with shorter program runtimes and lower memory usage”; Table I is introduced as examining “run time and memory usage,” but only its heading is present.

rows.title: A Simple Ricci Flow Proof of the Uniformization Theorem

errors.location: §3, proof of Theorem 3.2, immediately before (3.3)
errors.description: The proof claims one can choose sufficiently small A so the time-T isoperimetric lower bound is at least the logistic bound. Under the assumed violation, that comparison is impossible for small A, so (3.3) does not follow.
errors.evidence: The claimed comparison is equivalent to (κ(T)−1)/(κ(0)−1) ≤ e^(−BT)(4πA−κ(T)A²)/(4πA−κ(0)A²). As A→0, the fraction tends to 1 and B≥2, so the right side is at most e^(−2T)(1+o(1)); the contradiction hypothesis makes the left side strictly greater than e^(−2T). The text nevertheless asserts: “since the inequality (2.4) is tight for A → 0, we can choose A sufficiently small” to obtain that comparison.

errors.location: §2, Theorem 2.3 and §3, Proposition 3.1 proof
errors.description: The evolution equation and maximum-principle argument are not defined for I_A as introduced: for fixed A, (2.2) defines I_A as an infimum over curves, hence a scalar depending on A and t, with no r-variable or specified curve-dependent function to which the spatial derivative and maximum principle apply.
errors.evidence: Equation (2.2) defines I_A := inf_Λ L / inf_Λ̄ L̄, while (2.5) contains ∂²/∂r² ln I_A² and says r is the normal direction of Λ. Proposition 3.1 then applies the maximum principle directly to this I_A.

errors.location: Remark 2.2
errors.description: The displayed small-A expansion is incorrect: it omits the order-A^(3/2) correction to the square root, so the stated equality does not hold even up to o(A²).
errors.evidence: Expanding the preceding expression gives √(4πA−κA²) = 2√(πA) − κA^(3/2)/(4√π) + O(A^(5/2)). The manuscript instead writes √(4πA−κA³/(4√π)) + o(A²), whose correction to 2√(πA) is only order A^(5/2).

rows.title: Going Beyond Word Matching: Syntax Improves In-context Example Selection for Machine Translation

errors.location: Example Database and Test Set sections
errors.description: The manuscript does not report checking for overlap between WikiMatrix demonstrations and FLORES+ devtest source sentences. If test sentences or close duplicates occur in the retrieval database, they could be selected as demonstrations and inflate the reported gains attributed to syntax-based selection.
errors.evidence: “We adopt WikiMatrix v1 … as our example database” and “We perform our evaluation on the devtest set of FLORES+”; no cross-corpus overlap check or deduplication is described.

rows.title: Unveiling the biological effects of radio-frequency and extremely-low frequency electromagnetic fields on the central nervous system performance

errors.location: RF-EMR exposure effects on learning and memory
errors.description: The text identifies Son et al.’s subjects as rats, but reference 56 identifies the study as using 5xFAD mice. This misreports the study population.
errors.evidence: Text: “in a research conducted on rats by Son et al”; reference 56 title: “Long-term RF exposure on behavior and cerebral glucose metabolism in 5xFAD mice.”

errors.location: ELF-EMF section, paragraph on Ahlbom et al.’s pooled analysis
errors.description: The account appears to treat the proportions of children in exposure categories as evidence about their relative risks. Exposure prevalence alone does not establish risk; the text supplies no case/control counts or effect estimates supporting that inference.
errors.evidence: “99.2% of children residing in households with exposure levels below 0.4 μT exhibited a lower risk… In contrast, 0.8% of children exposed to 0.4 μT or higher displayed relatively elevated risk estimates.”

errors.location: Paragraph beginning “The nonthermal effects arise from forces acting on particles”
errors.description: The text generalizes that nonthermal effects arise from the pearl-chain effect, then identifies dielectric saturation as another nonthermal effect. Those statements are internally inconsistent: the latter is presented as a distinct mechanism, not as pearl-chain formation.
errors.evidence: “The nonthermal effects arise from forces acting on particles, known as the pearl chain effect.” Later: “Another nonthermal effect is the dielectric saturation…”

rows.title: A Simple, Nearly-Optimal Algorithm for Differentially Private All-Pairs Shortest Distances

errors.location: Lemma 3.1, proof
errors.description: The proof applies a concentration bound for a fixed sum of independent Laplace variables to the path selected by minimizing noisy edge weights. That path depends on the noise, so the sum along it is not a fixed Laplace sum; a union bound over vertex pairs does not control all candidate paths. The claimed error bound is therefore not established and can fail when there are many competing paths.
errors.evidence: “each distance … is the sum of a maximum of t edge weights” and “By Lemma 2.4” the error is bounded, followed by a union bound over “the n² released distances.”

errors.location: Lemma 4.4, statement and proof
errors.description: The stated lower bound can exceed the maximum possible size |A_i|≤n for allowed parameters. For n=2^m, k=m and i=1, the proof's threshold (t/4)n^(1-2/k) is asymptotically 12.5n log(n), which is greater than n. Thus Lemma 4.4 as stated is false, and subsequent arguments relying on that bound are unsupported.
errors.evidence: The manuscript allows k=⌊log(n)/log(2)⌋ and claims “|A_i| ≥ (t/4) · n^{1-(i+1)/k} for all i”; it sets t=⌈100·n^{1/k}log(n)⌉.

errors.location: Lemma 4.4, proof
errors.description: The proof treats the size of the union of t fixed-size uniform samples as Binomial(n,p_i). Within each round, inclusion indicators for distinct vertices are dependent because the sample size is fixed, so this distributional claim does not hold and the cited binomial Chernoff bound does not justify the stated tail probability.
errors.evidence: “Let X_i ∼ Binomial(n,p_i) be the number of vertices in A_i” followed by an application of Lemma 2.5.

errors.location: Construction 2, formation of T; Theorem 4.3 proof
errors.description: The trees and their clusters depend on private edge weights: cluster membership and shortest-path trees are defined using d_G. The proof then composes per-tree releases as if the trees were fixed across neighboring inputs. The cited tree-release guarantee for a fixed tree does not account for this data-dependent choice, so the claimed DP guarantee is not established.
errors.evidence: Clusters are defined using “d(w,u)” and T_i^r is formed from “the shortest path tree centered at w”; the proof then claims privacy by running the Corollary 4.1 mechanism on each T.

errors.location: Appendix C, proof of Theorem 4.2; Appendix D, proof of Theorem 4.4
errors.description: The per-tree privacy parameter is set to ε/(2√2·q·log(2/δ)), where q is the number of trees, but Lemma 2.2 uses ε/(2√(2q log(2/δ))). The stated parameter is substantially smaller for these q, so the tree-release error scales with q·log(2/δ), not the claimed √(q·log(2/δ)). The claimed additive bounds do not follow from the mechanisms specified in these proofs.
errors.evidence: Appendix C specifies “ε/(2√2(k n^{1/k}) log(2/δ))”-DP per tree while claiming an error proportional to √(k n^{1/k})√log(2/δ); Appendix D uses the analogous denominator with t·k.

errors.location: Theorem 4.1, parameter range and additive-error bound
errors.description: The theorem allows k=1, but its stated additive bound contains log(k), which is zero at k=1. It therefore claims zero additive error with probability 1−γ, despite specifying releases with nonzero Laplace noise; the bound cannot hold for the stated parameter range.
errors.evidence: Theorem 4.1 permits “k ∈ Z⁺” and gives additive error O(k·n^{1/k}·log^{2.5}(n)·log(k)·log(1/γ)/ε).

rows.title: HDRTransDC: High Dynamic Range Image Reconstruction with Transformer Deformation Convolution

errors.location: Analysis of Computational Budgets
errors.description: The reported cross-method inference-time comparison excludes homography computation for DeepHDR, so it does not compare the full image-generation pipelines and may understate that method’s runtime.
errors.evidence: The manuscript says inference time is measured while generating 15 images using a GPU, then states: “we do not consider the time consumption of homographies in DeepHDR.”

rows.title: A Strongly Subcubic Combinatorial Algorithm for Triangle Detection with Applications

errors.location: Theorem 2, Analysis, Case 2.1
errors.description: The argument does not establish that BFS⁺ detects the triangle when exactly one triangle vertex is at level 1. The other two vertices can be discovered earlier through different level-1 vertices, so scanning the edge between them does not by itself show the triangle is detected. The sampling bound therefore relies on an unproved claim that every sampled vertex in A succeeds.
errors.evidence: The text says: “Then b and c appear on the next level (level 2) of the BFS tree. Assuming that b is discovered before c, the triangle {a, b, c} is detected while scanning the adjacency list of b.” For example, with triangle abc and extra edges sa, sp, sq, pb, qc, a BFS from s can place a,p,q at level 1, with b discovered from p and c from q at level 2. The manuscript does not specify a BFS⁺ check that detects a triangle in this situation.

rows.title: A form of refined Roth's theorem and its application to the $abc$-conjecture

errors.location: Definitions of χ_v(x,∞); equations (6), (11), and (12)
errors.description: For a non-Archimedean place, χ_v(x,∞)=1/|x|_v makes the proximity contribution negative when x is divisible by the corresponding prime. This contradicts the stated counting formula (6) and prevents N(x,∞) from being the nonnegative count used later. For κ=Q, S={∞}, and x=p^k, the definition gives a contribution −k log p at p, while (6) gives an empty sum plus O(1).
errors.evidence: “If v is non-Archimedean, set … χ_v(x,a)=… 1/|x|_v : a=∞”; equation (6) sums only over v with ord_v(x⁻¹)>0.

errors.location: Proof of Theorem 1.4, paragraph beginning “By using Dirichlet's unit theorem”
errors.description: The asserted uniform comparison between the absolute values of an algebraic integer at all Archimedean places is false, even for units. In Q(√2), powers of 1+√2 have embedding absolute values whose ratio grows without bound. Thus the claimed O(1) bound for m(y,0) does not follow; for those powers, the contribution from the embedding of absolute value √2−1 grows linearly with the exponent.
errors.evidence: “there exists a constant c(κ) such that |y|_v ≤ c(κ)|y|_w for any Archimedean v, w”; the proof then concludes “m(y,0)=…=O(1).”

errors.location: Theorem 2.1 statement and its construction of x′; Proof of Theorem 1.5
errors.description: Theorem 2.1 requires a single x′ that works for all but finitely many x, but the subsequent construction chooses ideals from the prime factorization of x and x−a_j, so the resulting x′ depends on x. This matters in Theorem 1.5: for κ=Q, a₁=0, a₂=1, and simple x=1/p, the claimed y=(x−a₁)(x−a₂)/x′ cannot be integral for all sufficiently large primes p if x′ is fixed, since its denominator contains p² and a fixed rational x′ can cancel only finitely many such primes.
errors.evidence: Theorem 2.1: “There exist an extension field K … and an element x′∈K such that all but finitely many x∈κ”; the later construction defines ideals using “(x)” and “(x−a_j)”; Theorem 1.5 asserts “y=1/(x′Q(x)) is an algebraic integer.”

errors.location: Proof of Theorem 1.6, equations (21)–(22)
errors.description: The proof uses the wrong sign and therefore applies Theorem 1.5 at the wrong second finite point. Under the stated relation a+b=c and x=a/c, the second point is 1 because x−1=−b/c; the proof instead uses −1 and then identifies x+1 with b/c. Its separate assertion a+b+c=0 also conflicts with the theorem's stated equation.
errors.evidence: Theorem 1.6 assumes “a+b=c”; the proof says “Since a+b+c=0” and applies (12) at x=a/c with points 0 and −1, then equates the −1 count to the primes dividing b.

rows.title: A missing theorem on dual spaces

errors.location: Theorem 3.3, proof (1)
errors.description: The proof gives the wrong sign for the square of the predual map. From J* = L_i and L_i² = -I, duality implies (J²)* = -I and therefore J² = -I, not J² = I. The printed conclusion contradicts the required criterion for a complex structure.
errors.evidence: “It is easy to see by duality theory that J² = I (since (J²)* = -I).”

rows.title: Algebraic description of complex conjugation on cohomology of a smooth projective hypersurface

errors.location: Example 2.4
errors.description: The claimed basis is for the entire quotient, which is infinite-dimensional.
errors.evidence: The text claims {[1], [yu]} is a basis of Q[y,x0,x1,x2]/Jac(S). Setting all x_i to zero sends every generator G and yG_i of Jac(S) to zero, so this quotient surjects onto Q[y], and cannot have a two-element basis.

errors.location: The definition of μ preceding Example 2.8; Example 2.8
errors.description: The displayed formula forces μ=0, so the example's proposed real-cohomology description omits the conjugate Hodge component.
errors.evidence: The numerator is (∫γ1 ω)(∫γ2 ω) − (∫γ2 ω)(∫γ1 ω), which is zero by commutativity. Thus Example 2.8 reduces to C[1], while [1] lies in H^{1,0} and the elliptic curve also has a nonzero H^{0,1} component.

errors.location: Theorem 2.3, displayed conclusion
errors.description: As written, the theorem equates nonzero classes in distinct Hodge summands.
errors.evidence: Theorem 2.1 sends wt i to H^{n−1−i,i} and wt n−1−i to H^{i,n−1−i}. For even n these are distinct summands; since U_k is a basis element, the displayed equality of their images cannot hold. The displayed conclusion needs a conjugation on one side to express the stated goal.

errors.location: Theorem 2.3 and its proof
errors.description: The stated freedom to choose any g is incompatible with identifying the unique conjugate class when the opposite Hodge summand has dimension greater than one.
errors.evidence: The theorem requires only that f_{j_i}g_{j_i} not lie in Jac(G), and the proof says it suffices to arrange the single scalar equality R(y^i f_{j_i}, y^{n−1−i}h_{j_i})=U_{k,γ}. One pairing value does not determine a vector in a higher-dimensional Hodge summand; changing g while preserving nonzero pairing generally changes the proposed class.

errors.location: Sections 2.4–2.5, odd n case
errors.description: The floor expression selects all middle-Hodge indices, making the claimed real-cohomology span too large when |I_m|>1.
errors.evidence: For the integer N=|I_m|, floor(N+1/2)=N. In the even-N branch of Corollary 2.7, each of these N middle indices contributes two real dimensions, giving 2s+2N, whereas μ=2s+N (with s=Σ_{i<m}|I_i|). For example, N=2 gives a span of dimension 2s+4 instead of 2s+2.

rows.title: CR functions at CR singularities: approximation, extension, and hulls

errors.location: Section 6, equations (24)–(25) and the sentence claiming that Q_n converges uniformly to f
errors.description: The Gaussian scale and normalization make Q_n tend to zero as n increases, rather than approximate f. Thus this argument does not establish the stated approximation result.
errors.evidence: The manuscript defines c_n by 1/c_n = ∫_C exp(−|ζ|²/n) dA(ζ), so c_n = 1/(πn). Since χf is supported in |ζ|≤ε, for bounded z the exponential kernel tends uniformly to 1 on that support; hence Q_n(z, z̄)=O(1/n) and tends uniformly to zero. This cannot converge to a nonzero f.

errors.location: Example 3.9, equation (5) and the claim that X is compact
errors.description: The displayed set X is not compact, so it does not provide the stated example of a compact set whose disc hull is noncompact.
errors.evidence: The points (1, φ_k(1), 1/k) belong to X. The sequence φ_k(1) is bounded, so a subsequence converges to some b; the corresponding points converge to (1,b,0), which is not in X because every point displayed in (5) has third coordinate 1/k>0.

errors.location: Example 3.13, equation (9)
errors.description: The asserted formula for DH(X) includes points arising from the boundary Im z₂=0 of the second component, even though that component requires Im z₂<0. In particular, (3/2,1) is included by (9) but is not in DH(X).
errors.evidence: An attached disc whose boundary lies in the second component has |φ₂|=1 on the boundary, so φ₂ is either constant or a finite Blaschke product. A nonconstant finite Blaschke product takes the boundary around the full unit circle and cannot have boundary values only in Im z₂<0; thus φ₂ must be constant with Im φ₂<0. A disc attached to the first component has |φ₁|=1 on the boundary and therefore |φ₁|≤1 inside. Neither type can contain (3/2,1), although equation (9) includes it.

errors.location: Theorem 8.1 proof, first disc construction following equation (28)
errors.description: The stated condition defining A₁ does not ensure that the positive real λ required by the construction exists, so the claimed inclusion A₁⊂DH(A₀) is not proved by this construction.
errors.evidence: For C>3, p=(1,i,−2i) satisfies (28): Im(ω·conjugate(ξ₁)·ξ₂)=0, Re(...)=2≥|ξ₁ξ₂|²=1, and the size bounds hold. But the proof requires λ²=wz₁/z₂=−2, which has no positive real solution. Also p∉A₀, since −2i≠conjugate(1)·i=i.

rows.title: Efficient Fault-Tolerant Single Qubit Gate Approximation And Universal Quantum Computation Without Using The Solovay-Kitaev Theorem

errors.location: Method, Eqs. (4) and (6)
errors.description: The claimed real-vector equation does not ensure the physical phase is constant across codewords, so the asserted logical gate need not preserve the code space. In Eq. (5), for logical zero and a=1,b=0,c=1, the bit string is 0101101; Eq. (6) applies phase e^{i2α} to it, while the a=b=c=0 term 0000000 receives phase 1. For α=π/4 these phases differ, so Eq. (6) does not implement the claimed logical P(α). The issue is that binary XOR combinations of generator rows are not ordinary real linear combinations.
errors.evidence: Eq. (4) asserts that any real solution of Hv=w yields P(α)_L; Eq. (6) gives P(−α)⊗P(α)⊗1^⊗4⊗P(α).

errors.location: Introduction, paragraph beginning “How to execute gates”; Conclusions, opening and final paragraphs
errors.description: The stated code-family assumptions do not make transversal S a valid logical operation for every self-orthogonal code. For example, C=span{1100} is self-orthogonal, but on its code state (|0000⟩+|1100⟩)/√2, applying S to each qubit gives (|0000⟩−|1100⟩)/√2, which is outside the code space stabilized by X(1100). Thus self-orthogonality alone does not support the claim that S is automatically fault-tolerant for the described family.
errors.evidence: “Consider a classical linear self-orthogonal binary code C”; “Using Steane-like code, the logical Z, H, X, S and CNOT are automatically FT.”

errors.location: Conclusions, final paragraph
errors.description: The printed value of m does not provide a phase grid fine enough to approximate arbitrary angles to ε. As ε tends to zero, the displayed quotient ε/[log₂(1/ε)⋯] tends to zero, so its ceiling is 1 for sufficiently small ε. The resulting dyadic phase grid has spacing π/2, which cannot approximate arbitrary phases to arbitrarily small ε.
errors.evidence: “where m = ⌈ϵ/ [log₂(1/ϵ) log₂ log₂(1/ϵ)···]⌉.”

errors.location: Conclusions, opening paragraph
errors.description: The stated gate-count bound O(ε log[1/ε] log log[1/ε]⋯) tends to zero as ε→0, contradicting the manuscript’s own Ω(log[1/ε]) lower bound. As printed, it cannot be a valid asymptotic gate-count bound for arbitrary single-qubit gates.
errors.evidence: The introduction states “at least Ω(log[1/ε])”; the conclusion claims “O(ϵ log[1/ϵ] log log[1/ϵ] ···) gates.”

rows.title: Every Polish group has a non-trivial topological group automorphism

errors.location: Proof of Theorem 1.1, paragraph beginning “Since U does not contain non-trivial linear combinations…”
errors.description: The extension that fixes every element of Y is not shown to be well-defined. It requires the automorphism of L to agree with the identity on L ∩ span(Y), but the proof establishes only that U itself contains no nonzero element of L. Maximality gives U ⊆ span(Y), not span(Y) ∩ L = {0}; finite sums of elements of U may lie in L. Consequently, the prescribed map can assign conflicting images to an element of L ∩ span(Y).
errors.evidence: The proof says “every t ∈ U \ {0_G} is Z₂-linearly independent from {x_i},” then takes maximal independent Y ⊆ U, and claims it can “extend it to a Z₂-automorphism of H by setting φ(y) = y for y ∈ Y.” The stated properties do not establish that L and span(Y) intersect trivially or that φ fixes their intersection.

rows.title: Explicit expression and fast algorithms for the inverse of some matrices arising from implicit time integration

errors.location: Theorem 2.4 proof, equation (2.18)
errors.description: The displayed identity for Hᵀ is false for the general distinct nodes allowed by the theorem: its right-hand side has superdiagonal entries c₁,…,cₙ, whereas Hᵀ has entries 1,…,n. The next displayed computation uses Dₙ instead of Cₙ, which does give the required entries.

errors.location: Lemma 2.1, i≠j branch of the displayed identity in Crop 7
errors.description: The product on the right-hand side omits only k=j, but the derivative on the left requires omitting both k=i and k=j. The supplied proof later gives the latter, correct product.
errors.evidence: Take n=1, c₀=0, c₁=2, i=0, j=1. The left side is ψ′(c₁)=1; the displayed right side ∏_{k≠j}(c₁−cₖ)=2. The proof following equation (2.7) instead gives ∏_{k≠i,j}(c_j−c_k)=1.

errors.location: Introduction statement identifying the BIM inverse with Wₙᵀ; Section 2.2 displayed formula for N
errors.description: The two supplied claims for the BIM inverse disagree: the introduction identifies it as Wₙᵀ for cᵢ=i, while the later expression for N adds Dₙ⁻¹ to a term that equals Wₙᵀ.
errors.evidence: For n=1, c₀=0, c₁=1, Wₙᵀ=[1]. The displayed formula gives N=[1·(1·1·1·1)+1]=[2], so N≠Wₙᵀ.

rows.title: Fields of definition of dynamical systems on $\mathbb{P}^{1}$. Improvements on a result of Silverman

errors.location: Lemma 4, proof of the converse
errors.description: The proposed semilinear automorphism does not follow from the conjugacy equation and is not generally in the centralizer of φ. Given φ^σ = f φ f⁻¹ and φ^σ = τσ φ τσ⁻¹, the lift that commutes with φ is f⁻¹ ∘ τσ; the proof instead claims τσ ∘ f⁻¹ does so. This leaves the converse, and thus the stated proof of the exact sequence, invalid as written.
errors.evidence: The proof states: “Since φ^σ = f ∘ φ ∘ f⁻¹, this implies that τσ ∘ f⁻¹ is an element of 𝒩φ mapping to σ.” But (f⁻¹ ∘ τσ) φ (f⁻¹ ∘ τσ)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ φ^σ f = φ, whereas the claimed composition does not generally satisfy this identity.

rows.title: From Tripods to Bipods: Reducing the Queue Number of Planar Graphs Costs Just One Leg

errors.location: Section 3, quadrangular-face iterative step
errors.description: The conditions for both optional attachments refer to an edge from the new bag to Bₓ₃ and add an edge to x₂. As written, e₄ never adds the x₄ attachment needed for the subsequent subdivision of C₁₄₃ into faces f₁₄ and f₄₃. This leaves the claimed construction and face analysis unsupported in this case.
errors.evidence: “if there is an edge e₂ = (vₖ₊₁, v₂), where v₂ ∈ Bₓ₃, we also connect xₖ₊₁ to x₂. Similarly, if there is an edge e₄ = (vₖ₊₁, v₂), where … v₂ ∈ Bₓ₃, we also connect xₖ₊₁ to x₂.” The following text uses e₄ to split C₁₄₃ and create f₁₄ and f₄₃.

errors.location: Lemma 3.7 proof
errors.description: The path P is defined with d vertices, but the proof uses it for d+1 layers indexed 0 through d, including p₀, which is undefined. Thus the stated embedding construction does not assign product coordinates to every layer.
errors.evidence: “let P = (p₁, p₂, …, p_d)” followed by “for a fixed layer i ∈ {0, …, d}” and references to pᵢ.

errors.location: Claim 4.12 proof
errors.description: In the case x ≠ x′ and y ≠ y′, the two candidate edges in H corresponding to the nesting pair are (x,y) and (x′,y′). The proof instead invokes (x,y) and (y,y′); since it has already established y ≠ x′, this is not the second candidate edge. The cited non-nesting property therefore does not establish the claim for this case.
errors.evidence: “If x ≠ x′ and y ≠ y′, we obtain that the order … corresponds to … x, x′, y, y′. As edges (x, y), (y, y′) do not nest in H_h…”

rows.title: How to surpass no-go limits in Gaussian quantum error correction and entangled Gaussian state distillation?

errors.location: Gaussian quantum information, covariance matrix definition before Eq. (2)
errors.description: The stated matrix is not the usual real symmetric covariance matrix: for the vacuum, tr(ρq̂p̂)=i/2 and tr(ρp̂q̂)=-i/2. Using these unsymmetrized moments also makes Eq. (2) fail for general nonsymplectic Gaussian channels unless an additional commutator term is included.
errors.evidence: “the (j, k)-th entry of γ(ρ) is γ(ρ)ⱼ,ₖ = tr(ρx̂ⱼx̂ₖ)” followed by Eq. (2), which specifies real M and symmetric N.

errors.location: Eq. (4), two-mode squeezed vacuum
errors.description: The state coefficients have the wrong sign for the squeezing operator defined in the manuscript. Expanding that operator at r=0 gives |00⟩−r|11⟩+O(r²), whereas Eq. (4) gives |00⟩+r|11⟩+O(r²).
errors.evidence: The operator is defined as Ŝⱼ,ₖ(r)=e^{r(âⱼâₖ−âⱼ†âₖ†)}, but Eq. (4) assigns coefficients +tanhⁿ(r).

errors.location: Lemma 4 and the claims about implementing the partial transpose of a balanced beam splitter
errors.description: The partial-transposed beam-splitter matrix Z₂BZ₂=2⁻¹ᐟ²[[I,Z],[-Z,I]] is not symplectic: its transformed q̂₁ and p̂₁ commute. With N=0, it therefore does not define a deterministic Gaussian unitary or CPTP Gaussian channel, despite the text presenting its implementation with displacement recovery as a physical operation.
errors.evidence: The manuscript states that the partial transpose “can [be] effectively implement[ed]” by gate teleportation and defines Bᵢ at the covariance-map level, while also noting that the resulting matrix “is not symplectic.”

errors.location: Application, statement following Eq. (17)
errors.description: The numerical approximation of the stated threshold is incorrect: π³/(4√(2e)) is approximately 3.32, not 1.012. This gives an erroneous numerical bound for the noise range described as typical.

rows.title: Large Bricks and Join-irreducible torsionfree classes

errors.location: Proposition 3.9, paragraph beginning “Now by Lemma 3.8…”
errors.description: The spanning tree does not necessarily index a directed system, so Lemma 3.6 cannot be applied as claimed. Orienting its edges upward can leave vertices with no common upper bound in the tree, even when the original poset is directed. For example, a directed poset with covers a,b < c,d < e can have a spanning tree containing a–c, b–c, a–d, c–e; in that tree c and d have no common upper bound. The construction therefore does not establish the claimed lim→f-simple module containing every f-simple.
errors.evidence: The proof asserts that assigning maps along the spanning tree “gives a directed system of f-simples” and then applies Lemma 3.6, which assumes a direct system. Acyclic orientation alone does not make an indexing category directed.
